title: Deep Residual Learning (ResNet)
hook: Stacking more layers used to make networks worse, not better. ResNet's fix — let each layer learn a tweak to its input — unlocked nets over 100 layers deep.
key_points: Skip connections compute F(x)+x, so a layer learns a residual change rather than a full transformation.
This solved the degradation problem where very deep plain nets trained worse than shallow ones.
Enabled networks of 100+ (and even 1000+) layers that keep improving with depth.
Skip connections are now a default building block across architectures.
content_html: He, Zhang, Ren, and Sun noticed that simply stacking more layers made deep networks harder to train, not better. Their fix — residual or "skip" connections that let a block learn a small change to its input instead of a full mapping — let them train networks over 100 layers deep and win the ImageNet 2015 challenge.
extra_html:
How it works

A residual block computes F(x) + x: the layers learn F(x), the adjustment, and then the original input x is added back. If a block has nothing useful to add, it can simply push F toward zero and pass the input through unchanged. That gives gradients a clean shortcut path during backpropagation, so signal flows to early layers without vanishing — which is what makes very deep training stable.

Why it matters

ResNet showed that depth, done right, keeps paying off, and it removed the practical ceiling on how deep a network could be. The skip connection turned out to be a general trick: it shows up in Transformers, U-Nets, and most modern architectures, making ResNet one of the most influential ideas in deep learning.

related.hook: Re-center and re-scale each layer's activations on every minibatch, and deep nets suddenly train faster and tolerate much higher learning rates.

prereqs.hook: A neural net learns by asking, for every weight, 'how much did you contribute to my mistake?' Backprop answers all of them at once.
